hints: Look at where the original curve levels off to find Vmax, then think about what part of the enzyme a non-competitive inhibitor binds to and whether adding more substrate can overcome it.
Remember how Km is found from any curve - halve your new Vmax value and read across then down to the x-axis to get the estimate.
walkthrough:
What non-competitive inhibition does**
A non-competitive inhibitor binds at the allosteric site, not the active site. It changes the shape of the active site so fewer enzyme molecules are functional. Adding more substrate cannot reverse this, so the maximum rate $V_{max}$ must fall.

Why Km stays the same**
Affinity of the remaining functional active sites for substrate is unchanged. So the substrate concentration needed to reach half of the new $V_{max}$ is the same as before. Your new curve stays to the right side at low substrate but plateaus lower, and reading half the new $V_{max}$ gives $K_m$ of about 0.055 to 0.06 $mmol dm^{-3}$.
Final answer: Curve with same general shape as original but with lower Vmax, reaching plateau below 8 arbitrary units. Km unchanged at 0.055 to 0.06 $mmol dm^{-3}$.

hints: Focus on the mRNA triplet code - think about what must happen first at the ribosome for a polypeptide to start being built, and what must happen last for it to be released.
Recall the specific base triplets involved - which one codes for methionine to begin, and what is special about the triplets that end the chain in terms of amino acids and release factors.
walkthrough:
Start codon starts building**
A codon is three adjacent bases on mRNA. The start codon is the first codon translated when the small ribosomal subunit attaches. In mRNA it is AUG, which codes for methionine, so every new polypeptide begins with methionine.

Stop codon stops building**
A stop codon is one of three triplets UAA, UAG or UGA in mRNA. They do not code for any amino acid. Instead release factors recognise them, chain elongation stops and the completed polypeptide detaches from the ribosome.

Final answer: Start codon: triplet of bases (AUG in mRNA) that initiates translation, codes for methionine / first amino acid. Stop codon: triplet of bases (UAA, UAG or UGA in mRNA) that terminates translation, does not code for an amino acid, causes polypeptide release.

hints: Trace what is left after step 3 and step 5 - toxin stays held by capture antibody, then think about which added molecules remain after the wash removes anything not firmly attached to toxin.
walkthrough:
Building the sandwich**
After step 3 only toxin held by capture antibody is left. In step 4 detection antibody with attached HRP is added and binds to the exposed part of the toxin. Step 5 washes away any detection antibody not bound to toxin. So draw one detection antibody sitting on each toxin complex.
Final answer: Each toxin bound to capture antibody now also has a detection antibody (with HRP) bound on top, forming antibody-toxin-antibody sandwich. No free detection antibody remains.

hints: Compare the two Y-shapes in Fig. 6.3 side by side - look at where each one is fixed and what extra label one carries, and think why they must not compete for the same spot on the toxin.
walkthrough:
Spot the structural difference**
The capture antibody is stuck directly to the plastic well to trap toxin from solution. The detection antibody is free in solution and carries the HRP enzyme star label so it can generate colour later. They also must bind different epitopes so both can attach to the same toxin at once.

Final answer: Detection antibody has HRP / enzyme attached, capture antibody does not; or capture antibody is immobilised on well surface, detection antibody is not; or they bind to different sites / epitopes on the toxin.

hints: Start from Fig. 6.5 - with very little toxin, very little HRP stays in the well, so think about how much blue-green oxidised TMB will form and how that looks by eye.
Think about what a colorimeter actually measures when light passes through that solution, and how a pale solution differs numerically from a colourless blank.
Link that number to toxin amount - why a small but real absorbance value proves a weak positive rather than a negative.
Consider how to make the number truly quantitative, for example by comparing to known standards rather than just judging by eye.
walkthrough:
From toxin to colour**
Low toxin means only a little detection antibody-HRP stays bound after washing. With TMB in excess, little HRP oxidises only a little TMB, so only a very pale blue-green forms. By eye this looks almost colourless and could be misread as negative.

What the colorimeter adds**
A colorimeter shines light through the well and measures absorbance. More blue-green product absorbs more light. A pale solution gives a low but non-zero absorbance, while a true negative blank gives essentially zero.

Why this confirms a weak positive**
Because absorbance is proportional to concentration of oxidised TMB, which reflects amount of bound HRP and hence toxin, the instrument is objective and sensitive. It can separate a slight colour change from colourless, removing subjective by-eye error.

Making it quantitative**
By measuring standards of known toxin concentration to plot a calibration curve of absorbance against concentration, the absorbance of the sample can be read off to give an actual toxin concentration, not just positive or negative.

Final answer: Colorimeter measures absorbance / light absorption of reaction mixture. Paler blue-green / lower colour intensity gives lower absorbance reading. Lower absorbance indicates lower concentration of oxidised TMB / toxin. Low toxin positive gives small absorbance above blank / negative, whereas by eye colourless vs very pale blue-green cannot be distinguished reliably. Use of standards / calibration curve gives actual toxin concentration.
